The former Polish president and Nobel Peace Prize laureate called on the United States to take political action as a global leader and increase its support for Ukraine in the Jack Morton Auditorium Tuesday. Lech Walesa, who served as Poland’s president from 1990 to 1995, spoke with Elliott School of International Affairs Dean Alyssa Ayres, as part of her Global Perspective Series, to discuss the United States’ position in international affairs today. Walesa, who led Poland’s transition from communist rule to democracy after the fall of the Soviet Union, addressed the audience in Polish with an English translator, calling for greater cooperation among Western nations amid global challenges, like the war in Ukraine, and encouraged reforms in democratic countries to strengthen and solidify democracy worldwide. “I will beg you, even if I have to fall on my knees, that you return to your world leadership role,” Walesa said. “You cannot separate yourself from the world, and you cannot aid criminals because it’s un-American.” Walesa received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1983 for his work leading the Solidarity movement — an independent trade union that challenged communist rule and became a major force in Poland’s transition to democracy following nearly 44 years of Soviet influence. He said the United States retreating from its traditional leadership role in recent years has left European nations unsure about what “side” the country is on regarding Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, which has since caused over one million casualties. Walesa said the U.S. guaranteed Ukraine’s security when the country gave up its nuclear weapons in 1994, arguing the international community, including the United States, must work together now to protect Ukraine. “You have always been a world leader and a good one at that,” Walesa said, referring to the U.S. “So help me understand what is going on in your country now?” Walesa warned a Russian victory in Ukraine could shift the global balance of power, making Russia a leader in a potentially “unipolar world” — a global power structure in which a single state holds a disproportionate share of economic, military and cultural influence. He argued the United States should maintain an active role in international affairs rather than isolate itself. “Russia is close by,” Walesa said. “And as soon as we succeed in turning Russia to the right direction, then we can think about China. This is possible, but only under U.S. leadership.” Walesa argued technological advances have outgrown the ability of individual countries to counter global issues independently, calling for expanded cooperation through institutions like the United Nations, the European Union and the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. He said countries must establish global safeguards to keep pace with technological developments and prevent widespread harm. “Just look at AI,” Walesa said. “It’s a beautiful idea, but you need to manage this somehow because this will fall into the hands of crazy people who can let our world burn. And for this, we need global management.” Walesa also called for reforms to strengthen democratic institutions worldwide, arguing politicians often prioritize short-term solutions while in office to gain political support for reelection. He proposed that all elected leaders be limited to two five-year terms, allowing voters to recall elected officials through petitions and financial transparency to restore public confidence in democracy. “We are at a moment where we’ve turned democracy into its own caricature,” Walesa said. “Politicians think in terms of their constituencies and their terms in office because that is where their interest lies.” Walesa cited Russian President Vladimir Putin as an example of the risks of allowing leaders to remain in power for too long, saying that two five-year terms would not have given Putin enough time to build the “gangster state” he has now established. Ayres asked Walesa whether his views on LGBTQ+ rights had evolved since he said gay politicians should sit at the back of Poland’s parliament or “behind a wall” in 2013. Walesa did not address the question, instead discussing the relationships between rights and obligations. Walesa then discussed the role of religion in political life, saying his Christian faith helped guide him through dangerous periods of his activism in support of the Solidarity movement. When a student in the audience asked what book had most influenced his political life, Walesa responded with the Bible, describing it as a source of wisdom. Toward the end of the event, Walesa reflected on lessons from the Solidarity movement and said political action requires different skills today than it did during his generation’s struggle against communism. He encouraged students to learn foreign languages, expand their knowledge and find others who share their ideas. He said his generation relied on courage to challenge political authority, while younger generations must use their access to information and opportunities to make informed decisions. Walesa said the youth of today have the opportunity to influence the world’s direction but must be willing to act, urging students to participate in political life and elect representatives carefully. “If you have the will to do it, a better world awaits for you, and I sincerely believe in that,” he said.
